title: Introducing The Author
text: Introducing The Author R obin Wall Kimmerer is a Native American woman and a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. A professor of Environmental and Forest Biology at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry (SUNY-ESF) , Kimmerer’s courses include Land and Culture, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, Ethnobotany, Ecology of Mosses, Disturbance Ecology, and General Botany. Kimmerer makes an effort to combine her scientific passion for plants, forests, and biology with her native Potawatomi heritage and knowledge. She is the director of the Center for Native Peoples and the Environment , an initiative geared towards sharing of modern environmental science and traditional environmental knowledge. Born in 1953 in New York to Robert and Patricia Wall, Kimmerer grew up in a rural area where she interacted every day with plants in the garden, woods, or even the wetlands. This led to a deep and sustained interest in the diverse biological world around her. She thought of plants as companions and assigned them real-life roles that help people along. This attitude underwent a change when she went to college and adopted the scientific worldview of botany. She eventually turned to teach and began to mingle with indigenous knowledge holders. This inspired her to try to marry the two worldviews for a better understanding of plants. Kimmerer became a graduate in botany from SUNY-ESF in 1975, after which she was hired by Bausch & Lomb in the position of microbiologist. She worked there for a couple of years and then returned to her studies. She received her master’s degree in botany from the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1979. She also completed her Ph.D. in plant ecology in 1983, after which she began teaching at different places such as Transylvania University, Centre College in Kentucky, and eventually back home in SUNY-ESF. She also has an honorary M.Phil degree in Human Ecology from the College of the Atlantic. Kimmerer has published several scientific articles as well as two books on her subject. Her first book, Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses , was published in 2003 and received the John Burroughs Medal Award. Her second book is Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants , which was published in 2013 and is the recipient of the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award. Kimmerer’s family was a part of the exodus of Native Americans from their homelands to less fertile lands. Her grandfather, Asa Wall, was forcibly sent to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and deliberately and systematically uprooted from his people and traditional way of life. She tries to recover her lost heritage by communicating more with her community’s elders and holders of knowledge and by learning the Potawatomi language. She also ensures that she attends certain ceremonial events and is an enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. She is a proponent of Traditional Ecological Knowledge, which was first described by Fikret Berkes of the University of Manitoba as “a cumulative body of knowledge handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of living beings with one another and with their environment.” Kimmerer is also involved in projects involving helping her native Potawatomi tribe, the general Native American population, as well as the wider diaspora of non-white peoples in the USA. This includes sponsoring the Undergraduate Mentoring in Environmental Biology project, which helps non-white students by pairing them with faculty members. Another pet project of hers is the American Indian Science and Engineering Society, which is active in community outreach programs. She has also been involved with the Strategies for Ecology Education, Development and Sustainability project, Ecological Society of America Traditional Ecological Knowledge Section, and has even participated in a discussion at a United Nations meeting on ecology.
